# If You Want to Kill Yourself

Maybe you're reading this with a plan, or the means, close by. Then before anything else, get another human being involved, and put some distance between you and the means. A crisis line or an emergency number counts, and the person on the other end can be a total stranger. Do the same if you can't stop yourself, or you're badly disoriented or intoxicated. Can't tell if that's you? Treat it like it is. This isn't me answering whether life is worth living. It just keeps the question open long enough to look at.

Then, before getting all philosophical, make sure there's a real, live grown-up in the room or on the phone, if that's possible. And as for the internal psychology of it, when the part that wants to die feels like all of you, go ahead and notice who's doing the noticing (as we discussed in Noticing Counts), or borrow an adult from the adult lending library in your head :). Any part of you that can help keep your body safe, or would rather wait on a decision you can't undo, is welcome. And if none of them shows up yet? No problem, the questions can wait.

Then ask: what is the self you want to kill? Is that self the same thing as your body? Why? Do you have the same body in dreams? What exactly do you expect your body's death to accomplish? If the problem is a state of mind, like self-hatred or despair, shame or loneliness, what makes you so sure that destroying the body ends it?

Buddhism, for one, won't let you off that easy. Death isn't an off switch there, and it isn't the new-age version either, where you get a free get-out-of-jail card back to the source. The way Buddhism sees it, the mind leans toward whatever you keep thinking and intending, and dying doesn't straighten it out. That lean carries right on through death and rebirth. Hell realms are possible too (not exactly the brochure). A human birth is the rare one, where you get a real shot at understanding suffering and ending what causes it. You don't have to believe any of that.

But if you're still weighing your life against the opposite claim, look into that claim first (and if you're at the edge right now, the first step above comes before any of this). Near-death experiences and seriously studied rebirth reports can't give you reliable odds about death. What they can do is shake the certainty that destroying the body guarantees nothing comes after.

You can see that momentum within this life, too. Rumination feeds rumination, and isolation can deepen despair. The more you hate yourself, the better your mind gets at it. Physical life keeps handing you redirections, though, like other people and things you have to do, and help when you reach for it. If the many traditions and the accumulating scientific evidence are right that the mind's causal process goes on after the body dies, killing the body may take away some of those redirections without taking away the suffering.

So, if everything's already on the table, what's the change you still can't bring yourself to make? Leaving? Quitting? Moving? Telling your family who you really are? Those aren't free, and you can't always take them back, but they're smaller than dying, and they can wait until you're calmer and have some help. Look at that life you've been afraid to change while you still have a human body, and people around to help redirect the path.

## How Much Happiness Do You Know Is Possible?

Part of love is wanting someone to be well, and how far that wish can reach depends partly on what kind of happiness you know is possible. If the happiness you know is food, safety, affection, friends, work that means something and some help when you need it, then wanting those things for somebody is love. Babies get some of this already. Practical love matters a lot.

Then a big spiritual experience comes along and shows you a peace or a love you didn't know existed, and "I want you to be happy" suddenly means a lot more. It's like finding out the house has a whole upstairs. That's partly why loving-kindness meditation can sound almost silly to someone who's never been up there, and so powerful to someone who has. You can say "may you be happy" a thousand times and mean about as much as "have a nice day." The practice is one way of finding that bigger love, and growing it.

If you're curious about that bigger happiness, follow the curiosity. No pretending to believe anything. There's a lot to read from all kinds of traditions. And there are people whose lives make you wonder what they found (you might know one already). Then look at the fruits. Is their path making them kinder and braver about suffering, or mostly just surer they've got the right explanation?

Sometimes care isn't the main thing missing. A meal can help, and so can a boundary or a kind sentence, but is that actually targeting the deeper existential question underneath? Life shouldn't be just something you endure, like a hamster wheel or a rat race. What would you need to bring zest to a life of discovery?

Curiosity can be enough here, something like "Other people say they've felt a depth of love or peace that I never have. I don't know if I believe their explanation. But what if the experience is possible for me?" Don't assume the limits of what you've felt so far are the limits of what's possible.
